forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough has government approval to capitalise £9.7m of costs; SEND report raises further support
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council has agreed with government to capitalise £9.7m of extraordinary day-to-day spending pressures under exceptional financial support, permission from government to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The medium-term financial strategy before Cabinet on 27 October 2026 says the sum is made up of £4.0m for 2025/26 and £5.7m for 2026/27.

The approval followed a review by the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA), published on 18 August. The strategy says the review found significant improvements in financial management and governance, and that challenges remain, including rebuilding reserves and pressures in children's social care.

A separate Cabinet report on reform of support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) says the council would need to consider exceptional financial support again. It links this to the council's low reserve balances and to the possibility that the Department for Education funds only 90% of future deficits. The report says "the Council would need to consider Exceptional Financial Support to fund this", meaning the remaining 10%.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough forecasts £7.9m overspend on £258m budget, £7.7m of it in children's services
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council expects to spend £7.9m more than planned in 2026/27 on its day-to-day running costs (revenue spending: staff, services and contracts). That is 3.1% over a net budget of £258m, according to a first-quarter report to its cabinet on 1 October. Children and Young People accounts for £7.7m of the total.

The largest single line is placements for children in care, forecast to overspend by £5.2m. The budget assumed 429 children in care and 41 residential placements. The number of children in care was 444 in June, and residential placements stood at 47 in August. The average price of the last ten residential placements is £9,000 a week against £6,500 budgeted, and nine children are in placements costing more than £10,000 a week. Residential care makes up £3.2m of the £5.2m placement overspend.

If the overspend continues to the year end, the council will have to draw on its general fund reserves, the money set aside as a cushion for the unexpected. The report forecasts the balance falling from £10.5m at the start of the year to £6.7m by 31 March 2027, a 36% reduction. Total usable reserves, money the council can actually spend, are £23.7m, excluding the deficit on schools funding. Of that, £6.8m, or 29%, is ringfenced for specific purposes.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough schools grant forecast to overspend by £16.6m in 2026/27, taking deficit to £17.7m
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council expects to overspend its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) by £16.6m in 2026/27, according to the first-quarter budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) presented to Cabinet on 1 October. That would leave a cumulative deficit of £17.7m by 31 March 2027.

The report attributes the overspend to increased demand for Education, Health and Care Plans, the legal documents that set out support for children with special educational needs and disabilities. This spending falls under high needs, the part of school funding for those children.

The Department for Education (DfE) has committed to fund 90% of deficits held at 31 March 2026. For deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28, the paper quotes the government as saying: "local authorities can expect that we will continue to take an appropriate and proportionate approach, though it will not be unlimited." From 2028/29, the report says, spending on special educational needs and disabilities is to be covered within the government's departmental expenditure limit, its fixed spending budget for departments. The papers do not say how much of the new deficit the government will fund.

findings.headline: The Commissioner's proposed 2027/28 precept is to be presented to the Panel on 26 January 2027, after central grant allocations are published in December.
findings.detail: The paper sets out the timetable: central funding allocations in December, a precept survey after the financial analysis, and a proposed precept presented to the Panel in January. The Commissioner will then discuss the budget implications with the Chief Constable.
findings.matters: The precept and the funding settlement together set the force's revenue position for the year, and other councils and lenders will track the same timetable.
findings.figures: Central funding announcement due 18 December; precept to Panel on 26 January 2027
findings.quote: The Commissioner will then present to the Panel his proposed precept for 2027/28 on 26 January 2027.

findings.headline: Police officer costs are 39% (£85m) of the budget, against 38% (£80m) in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper gives officer costs as a share of the budget and in cash terms, showing an increase in both. It sets this alongside police staff costs, which are 15% (£33m) of the budget.
findings.matters: Staff costs make up most of the budget, so their growth limits the room for savings in other lines.
findings.figures: 39% (£85m) of the budget; 38% (£80m) in 2025/26; police staff 15% (£33m)
findings.quote: Police officer costs are 39% (£85m) of the budget. In 2025/26 these costs accounted for 38% (£80m) of the budget.

findings.headline: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough population is forecast to reach 1.078m residents by 2041, from 942k in 2025.
findings.detail: The paper says the population used for funding is based on a 2011 census uplift and has not kept pace with growth. It says the Constabulary would need an additional 15 officers every year to 2041 to maintain current service levels.
findings.matters: A funding formula that lags population growth affects every council using population-based allocations, and the gap is quantified here.
findings.figures: 1.078m residents by 2041; 942k residents in 2025 (ONS mid-2025); 15 additional officers every year to 2041
findings.quote: with our population forecast to increase to 1.078m residents by 2041

findings.headline: Opportunities for further efficiencies without a sacrifice in service "remain challenging difficult to identify".
findings.detail: The paper says the Constabulary's existing strategic steps (collaboration, procurement and other measures) have already been taken. It says the remaining opportunities to find efficiencies without a reduction in service are hard to identify, and that procurement is more likely to limit cost increases than to deliver significant savings.
findings.matters: A force that has already exhausted the usual efficiency levers is a useful reference for other councils planning savings beyond collaboration and procurement.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs are 3.6% (£7.9m) of the budget, against 2.7% (£5.4m) in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper gives capital financing costs as a share of the budget and in cash terms for the current year and 2025/26. It says the scope to reduce them lies in slowing some projects, but operational requirements and the sustainability agenda must still be met.
findings.matters: A rise in the revenue cost of capital financing reduces the budget left for services, and the same pressure will be felt by other councils with rising borrowing.
findings.quote: Capital financing costs to support the capital programme (the built estate, ICT, fleet) is 3.6% (£7.9m) of the budget.

daily_post.headline: The council is the subject of a paused Local Government Reorganisation and will remain responsible for local services for at least one additional MTFS year.
daily_post.lead: A finance director elsewhere in a two-tier or reorganising area would want to know how the pause changes the timetable for stable baselines and transition funding.
